---
title: "Origins"
description: >-
  zotLook is a fork of Guillaume Chapron's Zotero7QuickLook: what survives of it, why a fork rather than a contribution, and what it cost.
---

## This fork

**zotLook is a fork of [Zotero7QuickLook](https://github.com/gchapron/Zotero7QuickLook)
by Guillaume Chapron**, from whom the code and the MIT licence come. It is
maintained and developed further by [fre-ms](https://github.com/fre-ms).

A good deal of Chapron's work is still in place. Measured against the last
upstream commit, counting only lines that are neither blank, a comment nor a
brace: **45 %** of the JavaScript and **52 %** of `bootstrap.js` survive
verbatim, and 20 of the original 28 methods are still present under their own
names. The plugin has grown around them — those surviving lines are about a
nineteenth of what is here today. The figures come from `tool/provenance.mjs`,
and the test suite fails when they drift from what this page says.

The architecture is his throughout:

- the bootstrap-plus-singleton shape
- the capture-phase key listener on the items tree that gets in front of
  Zotero's own Space handler
- holding the preview subprocess open so a second press dismisses it
- the temp-directory strategy
- resolving a synced attachment before previewing it
- the ideas behind both the EPUB-to-HTML conversion and the contact sheet

The plugin ID is `zotlook@fre.ms`, distinct from Chapron's, so the two install
side by side rather than over one another.

## Why a fork

Nearly half of Chapron's lines are still here, and the architecture is his
throughout. Why not contribute to his project rather than start a line of one's
own?

**The size of it.** What has been added cannot be offered as a pull request: two
further platform routes, a page renderer, the annotation pipeline, the EPUB
conversion with its contents list, a settings pane, a test suite. That is not an
addition but a different order of magnitude, and nobody is served by dropping
something like it on another project's doorstep as a proposal.

**The aim.** Chapron describes his plugin as *"A Zotero 7+ plugin **for macOS**"*
and builds it on `qlmanage`, the system's Quick Look command. That is a clear
and legitimate decision: a plugin that does exactly what it should on one
system. zotLook aims elsewhere — at all three — and that is not a better aim,
only a different one.

::: {.callout-note title="Cross-platform costs something"}
The contact sheet shows it most plainly. It was first drawn by a bundled Swift
program through PDFKit: **0.12 s for 30 pages**. What replaced it is the pdf.js
build Zotero already ships, which runs everywhere — **0.42 s** for the same
pages, four times as long.

The Swift program only ever ran on macOS. Keeping it would have meant two
renderers and two ways of drawing annotations that had to keep looking alike.
The decision went against speed — under an aim of "macOS only" it would have
gone the other way, and rightly.
:::

The four reasons, in the order of their weight:

1. **Cross-platform.** Previews on Linux and Windows, not only on macOS.
2. **Annotations in the preview.** Zotero keeps them in its database, so without
   this a preview shows an unmarked document. It was the gap asked about most
   often in the Zotero forums.
3. **Links from the contact sheet into the reader.** A click on a thumbnail
   opens that very page — which turns an overview into a tool.
4. **EPUB previews on every system.** None of the three system previews renders
   an e-book, so zotLook converts it itself.

The fork carries a plugin ID of its own so that both can be installed side by
side, and the MIT licence with Chapron's copyright notice unchanged. What is
built here is open to him — a good part of it is his code.

## Further back

Behind that stands [ZoteroQuickLook](https://github.com/mronkko/ZoteroQuickLook)
by Mikko Rönkkö, which brought Quick Look to Zotero 4–6 and gave this line of
plugins its purpose and its name.

::: {.callout-note title="The debt is one of idea, not of code"}
That plugin was a XUL overlay extension — `install.rdf`, `overlay.xul`, a
Windows `Bridge.exe`, an AppleScript and a Perl script — an architecture Zotero 7
abolished outright, so Chapron wrote a new plugin rather than porting the old
one.

Comparing the two directly bears that out: of 250 substantive lines in the
original, 28 also occur here, and every one of them is a line any plugin
writes — `return;`, `} else {`, `let path = item.getFilePath();`. Everything
else the two share is Zotero and DOM API names.
:::

Rönkkö is therefore credited as the originator of the idea, and is deliberately
**not** listed as an author of this code — the repository carries no licence,
and none was needed, because nothing was taken from it.
